policies.summary: For eminent domain purposes, siting wind turbines or solar generating equipment is not a public utility activity, so neither utilities nor developers may condemn land for these facilities.

Cities and counties decide siting of wind and solar through planning and zoning; a merchant generator built after 2001 that is not in a regulated rate base may opt out of Kansas Corporation Commission jurisdiction, so no state body sites these projects.

Cherokee County, Kansas adopted Resolution R-27-2025 on Dec. 22, 2025: a nine-month moratorium on approving requests to use county roads, resources or infrastructure for commercial renewable energy projects (wind turbines or solar panels generating power for sale), cryptocurrency mining, data centers, battery energy storage systems, new or unpermitted landfills and transfer stations, quarries and nuclear energy plants, and a ban on constructing any of these in the unincorporated county during the term. Resolution 11-2026, adopted June 8, 2026, re-adopted the same moratorium through March 31, 2027, while the county weighs a comprehensive plan and zoning.
restrictions.long_description: moratorium: no approval of requests to use county roads, resources or infrastructure for, and no construction of, any commercial renewable energy project (multiple wind turbines and/or solar panels generating power for sale and off-site use, including roads, turbine foundations, panels and lines), cryptocurrency mining operation, data center, battery energy storage system, new or unpermitted landfill or transfer station, quarry or nuclear plant in the unincorporated county. R-27-2025: nine months from Dec. 22, 2025. Resolution 11-2026: effective June 8, 2026, expires March 31, 2027. Fine up to $1,000 per day.

restrictions.description: In May 2023, the Barton County Commission voted to require any solar farm to be 6 miles away from Cheyenne Bottoms—a wetland complex with significant wildlife—and placed a moratorium on commercial solar projects until the end of the year.
restrictions.long_description: In May 2023, the Barton County Commission voted to require any solar farm to be 6 miles away from Cheyenne Bottoms—a wetland complex with significant wildlife—and placed a moratorium on commercial solar projects until the end of the year. In March 2024, the Commission approved an amendment to the zoning regulations, updating the zoning map of Barton County to reflect “an addition of a ‘no build’ zone around Cheyenne Bottoms as it pertains to the development of ‘Large Scale Non-Commercial Solar Energy Conversion Systems.

restrictions.description: In August 2021, Cherokee County adopted a 1-year moratorium on wind energy development.
restrictions.long_description: In August 2021, Cherokee County adopted a 1-year moratorium on wind energy development. In October 2022, county commissioners adopted a wind energy ordinance that limits turbine height to 440 feet at the highest blade, sets a 39 dBa noise limit during the evening, and sets a 5,250-foot setback requirement from the nearest property line.

restrictions.description: In response to NextEra Energy’s proposal to construct a wind farm, the Douglas County Commission issued a moratorium on wind farm development in December 2013, which lasted until April 2014.
restrictions.long_description: In response to NextEra Energy’s proposal to construct a wind farm, the Douglas County Commission issued a moratorium on wind farm development in December 2013, which lasted until April 2014. In 2022, Douglas County adopted a solar ordinance that limits cumulative solar farm acreage in the county to 1,000 acres and requires solar panels and arrays to be at least 500 feet from any existing residence. In May 2024, after a public hearing, the Commission voted to adopt new wind regulations that increased setbacks from property lines to 2,500 feet. About two-thirds of commenters at the public hearing expressed opposition to wind energy projects in the county, with some requesting a wind energy ban. Others argued that the regulations were excessive and that the setbacks would effectively prevent wind energy development. One frequent commenter was arrested on suspicion of interfering with the conduct of public business

restrictions.description: The Kearny County zoning regulations provide that wind energy conversion systems must be set back at least 2,000 feet from any property line.
restrictions.long_description: The Kearny County zoning regulations provide that wind energy conversion systems must be set back at least 2,000 feet from any property line. The regulations also limit the maximum height of turbines to 350 feet which may be increased to 400 feet if the applicant can show that the additional height will result in increased efficiency. In no case, however, can turbine height exceed 400 feet.

restrictions.long_description: In March 2022, the Labette County Commission voted to refuse signing any road agreements with industrial wind farm developers in response to widespread opposition.

restrictions.long_description: In August 2022, Leavenworth County adopted a wind ordinance that sets a 1,500-foot setback from property lines and a 200-foot tower height limit for wind turbines.

restrictions.long_description: Linn County adopted a moratorium on wind energy projects in June 2020, which was originally set to expire in December 2020 but ultimately extended through December 2021. In July 2023, the Linn County Commission voted to entirely ban commercial wind construction.

restrictions.long_description: On October 24, 2022, the Osage County Commission unanimously adopted a measure to prohibit any new commercial wind and solar projects within the county’s borders. The county allows only small wind and solar systems of 30 kW or less for on-site power generation.

restrictions.long_description: In the fall of 2022, the Pawnee County Commission enacted a 1-year moratorium on utility-scale commercial solar projects. In November 2023, they voted to extend this moratorium by an additional 3 years.

restrictions.description: In December 2021, the Reno County Commission banned wind development in all zoned areas of the county.
restrictions.long_description: In December 2021, the Reno County Commission banned wind development in all zoned areas of the county. The vote to ban wind development in certain areas of the county came three years after residents requested that the commission impose a moratorium on wind development, ostensibly in response to news that NextEra was purchasing leases for a potential wind farm in the county. As of December 2021, a moratorium on commercial wind development was scheduled to run through March 2022. As of February 2023, the county’s zoning regulations provide that, “[i]n order to provide for an incorporated city to extend its corporate boundary and increase its tax base, no turbine shall be located within 1 mile of an incorporated city boundary.” Wind farms are permitted, however, in a designated Commercial Wind Energy Conversion Systems District in the unincorporated part of the county.

restrictions.description: The Woodson County Board of County Commissioners has enacted a moratorium and prohibition on Commercial Renewable Energy Projects in the unincorporated area of Woodson County.
restrictions.long_description: The Woodson County Board of County Commissioners has enacted a moratorium and prohibition on Commercial Renewable Energy Projects in the unincorporated area of Woodson County. Specifically, the resolution directs the suspension of acting on any application for a Conditional Use Permit or permits for the erection and construction of any Commercial Renewable Energy Project (Section 1), prohibits the establishment of any such project (Section 3), and declares such establishment a violation of public interest while the resolution is in effect. No applications for Conditional Use permits shall be set for public hearing prior to 12 months from adoption (Section 2). The moratorium may be extended, terminated earlier, or amended by subsequent resolution (Section 5). The resolution “shall remain in effect until the end of February 2026” (Section 6). There are no stated conditions or exceptions limiting the prohibition to specific areas, prior approvals, or compliance status. The moratorium is currently in effect as of December 5, 2025.

restrictions.description: In September 2023, Sedgwick Country enacted a 6-month moratorium on solar applications as it considered new solar regulations.
restrictions.long_description: In September 2023, Sedgwick Country enacted a 6-month moratorium on solar applications as it considered new solar regulations. In March 2024, the Sedgwick County Commission extended the September 2023 moratorium on new commercial solar farms until September 2024. In August 2024, the county adopted new regulations, officially ending the moratorium. The new regulations prohibit solar projects from exceeding 1,500 acres in area; prohibit solar projects from being located in or on more than 6 contiguous sections of land; and require new solar projects be set back at least 2 miles from the nearest solar project.

projects.description: Clearway Energy's proposed Rainbow Springs Solar project in Cherokee County, Kansas was stopped for now by the county's December 2025 moratorium on new large-scale energy projects. Clearway said it was disheartened by the decision, which it said stifles economic development and encroaches on property rights, and that it would keep working with the county and partnering landowners to find a way forward.
Local community members opposed a proposed 300-MW solar project near Cheyenne Bottoms, the largest inland wetland in the United States.
projects.long_description: Local community members opposed a proposed 300-MW solar project near Cheyenne Bottoms, the largest inland wetland in the United States. Several public hearings attracted large crowds of opposition. The County Commission first approved a moratorium on all commercial-scale solar in May 2023, then in March 2024, the Commission adopted zoning changes that specify a no-build zone within the Cheyenne Bottoms Basin.

projects.description: In 2015, Calpine Corporation proposed a 200-MW wind project on 30,000 acres on a ridge in Eastern Anderson County.
projects.long_description: In 2015, Calpine Corporation proposed a 200-MW wind project on 30,000 acres on a ridge in Eastern Anderson County. A group called Landowners Against Windmills organized in opposition. The group argued that the county’s zoning director unlawfully allowed Calpine to construct a 328-foot weather monitoring tower without a special use permit, violating public notice requirements. The tower was subsequently destroyed by vandalism at a loss of $200,000. The project was apparently abandoned. As of February 2023, there are no Calpine projects in Kansas or public plans to build in Anderson County.

projects.description: In January 2017, nearly 60 residents of Sumner County filed a lawsuit to challenge the county’s approval of a conditional use permit for the 60-turbine, 150-MW Argyle Creek Wind Farm.
projects.long_description: In January 2017, nearly 60 residents of Sumner County filed a lawsuit to challenge the county’s approval of a conditional use permit for the 60-turbine, 150-MW Argyle Creek Wind Farm. In September 2017, a judge ruled against the Sumner County Commission, thereby blocking the project.

projects.description: In October 2022, Osage County Commissioners denied an application from Auburn Harvest Wind to construct a wind farm on 30,000 acres.
projects.long_description: In October 2022, Osage County Commissioners denied an application from Auburn Harvest Wind to construct a wind farm on 30,000 acres. At a hearing earlier in the month, local residents expressed concerns that the project would permanently alter the landscape and impact wildlife.

projects.description: Shortly after the plans for a 103-MW Chisholm Trail Solar Energy Center project was proposed, in September 2023, the County Commission implemented a ban on utility-scale solar development for 6 months.
projects.long_description: Shortly after the plans for a 103-MW Chisholm Trail Solar Energy Center project was proposed, in September 2023, the County Commission implemented a ban on utility-scale solar development for 6 months. In August 2024, the Commission implemented changes to its regulations, requiring a conditional use permit for any large-scale solar energy projects exceeding 40 acres.

projects.description: In March 2005, Spanish company Gamesa began developing a proposal for a 100-MW wind farm in northeast McPherson County.
projects.long_description: In March 2005, Spanish company Gamesa began developing a proposal for a 100-MW wind farm in northeast McPherson County. In August 2005, the county adopted a 6-month moratorium, which was ultimately extended through August 2006. The project appears to have been abandoned.

projects.description: The Hope Ridge wind project is a 334-MW wind project.
projects.long_description: The Hope Ridge wind project is a 334-MW wind project. Opposition to the wind project led to a civil lawsuit filed by residents against the County Commissioners, who approved the project by a 2-1 vote in November 2024. Residents filed a lawsuit in December 2024, alleging that the decision to approve the conditional use permit “did not follow the law and was unreasonable and unlawful.” [Note: As of January 2025, the litigation was still ongoing.]

projects.project_name: Kansas Sky Energy Center Solar Project
projects.description: In 2023, Evergy proposed the Kansas Sky Energy Center Solar Project, a 159-MW solar farm to be developed on approximately 1,103 acres in Grant Township near Lawrence, Kansas.
projects.long_description: In 2023, Evergy proposed the Kansas Sky Energy Center Solar Project, a 159-MW solar farm to be developed on approximately 1,103 acres in Grant Township near Lawrence, Kansas. The project developer sought a conditional use permit from the Douglas County Planning Commission. The Commission received approximately 50 comments on the project, 30 of which expressed opposition to it. Voices against the project focused on the need to preserve agricultural land. In December 2023, the Douglas County Planning Commission’s review ended in a split 4-4 vote on the permit application. In April 2024, the Commission unanimously voted to approve the conditional use permit. In May 2024, a group of opponents of the project brought a lawsuit in the Douglas County District Court alleging that the approval of the permit conflicts with the County’s comprehensive plan and solar regulations. In December 2024, the District Court Judge issued an injunction preventing any construction on the project until the litigation is resolved. In October 2025, the Douglas County Commissioners voted unanimously to approve five temporary business use permits (TBUs) allowing the developer to conduct environmental testing for the project subject to a number of conditions while the litigation remains pending.

projects.description: A proposed 68-turbine project south of Leon was canceled in 2005.
projects.long_description: A proposed 68-turbine project south of Leon was canceled in 2005. The Butler County Planning Commission unanimously recommended approval of the project but the County Commission rejected it.

projects.description: Plans by Apex Clean Energy to construct a 139-turbine, 300-MW wind farm in Neosho County were met with opposition from residents.
projects.long_description: Plans by Apex Clean Energy to construct a 139-turbine, 300-MW wind farm in Neosho County were met with opposition from residents. Objections to the project included concerns regarding the cost of the project and potential issues with regulating the wind farm due to the lack of a strong zoning ordinance. After Apex Clean Energy received a permit for the project, 45 landowners filed a lawsuit in federal court to stop the project as an anticipatory nuisance. The court denied the developer’s motion for judgment on the pleadings, finding that the plaintiffs adequately alleged a claim of anticipatory nuisance. In June 2020, the parties voluntarily stipulated to dismissal, and the project entered commercial operation in 2021.

projects.description: A proposed 80-turbine, 220-MW wind farm by NextEra encountered local opposition in Reno County.
projects.long_description: A proposed 80-turbine, 220-MW wind farm by NextEra encountered local opposition in Reno County. After the Reno County Planning Commission issued a negative recommendation, 233 residents submitted protest petitions, which forced a unanimous vote of the Reno County Commission. In June 2019, the County Commission voted 2-1 in favor of the project, but, without a unanimous vote, the permit could not be issued. In July 2021, the developer filed a lawsuit alleging that the protest petitions were invalid, but in May 2020, the court ruled against the developer. In August 2022, the state appellate court upheld the decision that the protest petitions were legally sufficient to force a unanimous decision.

projects.description: In 2022, NextEra proposed the 500-MW Jeffrey Solar Project to be developed on approximately 5,000 acres of land in southwest Jackson County.
projects.long_description: In 2022, NextEra proposed the 500-MW Jeffrey Solar Project to be developed on approximately 5,000 acres of land in southwest Jackson County. The project has faced strong local opposition over concerns about its impact on property values and potential to interfere with property usage. In January 2025, a group of local residents opposing the project filed a lawsuit in the Topeka District Court alleging violations of environmental federal statutes and seeking an injunction to stop the project moving forward. In July 2025, the lawsuit was dismissed without prejudice for lack of standing and failure to state a claim.
